subject: physics
question_text: Define the terms momentum and impulse. State and explain the law of conservation of linear momentum. Give its examples.

verification.note: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024), Unit 5 SHORT ANSWER. The mark split is invented and needs a Telangana IPE teacher; no exam appearance years are printed for this question, so appearances[] stays empty. AI physics check 2026-08-24: formulas, signs, numbers and claims verified against NCERT Class-11 conventions; corrections applied to explanation text (why / common_mistakes / memory_tip), marked answer lines unchanged unless factually wrong.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Momentum
lines: Momentum is the product of the mass and
It is a vector. SI unit: kg m/s.
steps.margin_note: Definition, formula, unit. Three short lines earn the mark cleanly.
steps.why: Momentum is the quantity that is conserved, so every later line in this answer rests on this one.
common_mistakes: Writing "momentum is mass into speed". It is velocity, so momentum has a direction.

recall.must_convey: That momentum is mass times velocity.

steps.memory_tip: Momentum = mass × velocity — the quantity every later line of this answer conserves.

steps.label: Impulse
lines: Impulse is the product of a force and
the time for which it acts.

lines.text: I = F × Δt = change in momentum

steps.margin_note: Add "= change in momentum". That equality is what makes impulse useful.
steps.why: A large force for a short time and a small force for a long time can deliver the same impulse — this is the idea behind shock absorbers and catching a ball.
common_mistakes: Giving the unit as newton. Impulse is a force MULTIPLIED by a time.

recall.must_convey: That impulse is force times the time it acts, and equals the change in momentum.
accept: I equals F into delta t

steps.memory_tip: Impulse = force × time = the change in momentum. A big force for a short time equals a small force for a long time.

steps.label: The law
lines: If no resultant external force acts on
a system, the total momentum of the
steps.margin_note: The condition "no external force" is half the law. A law stated without it is incomplete.
steps.why: Internal forces always come in equal and opposite pairs, so they cancel in the total. Only an outside force can change it.
common_mistakes: Dropping the "isolated system" condition and stating momentum is always conserved.

recall.must_convey: That with no external force acting, the total momentum of a system stays constant.
accept: no external force so total momentum is constant
momentum of an isolated system is conserved
external force lekapothe total momentum constant

steps.memory_tip: Say the condition with the law: the total momentum is constant WHEN no external force acts.

steps.label: The shell example
steps.margin_note: A two-piece sketch with the two velocity arrows. Draw it — it explains the minus sign faster than a sentence.
steps.why: The picture shows what the algebra says: the two momenta point opposite ways, which is the only way they can add to zero.
common_mistakes: Drawing both arrows the same way, which contradicts the equation written beside it.

recall.must_convey: That a figure of the two pieces with opposite velocity arrows is drawn.

steps.memory_tip: Draw the shell: one arrow left, one arrow right. The magnitudes m₁v₁ and m₂v₂ are equal; with signs, m₁v₁ = −m₂v₂.

steps.label: Worked example
lines: A shell at rest bursts into two pieces.
The momentum before is zero, so:
The pieces fly in opposite directions.
steps.margin_note: One worked example is worth more than four named ones. Take it to the minus sign.
steps.why: The example is where the law does visible work: knowing only that the shell started at rest fixes the direction of both pieces.
common_mistakes: Listing examples by name without showing the momentum equation for any of them.

recall.must_convey: That a shell at rest bursting into two pieces gives m₁v₁ = − m₂v₂.
accept: shell at rest bursts into two pieces
shell rendu mukkalu ga break aithe
reject: no external force so total momentum is constant

steps.memory_tip: Start from zero: the total momentum is 0 before the burst, so the two pieces carry equal and opposite momenta.

steps.label: More examples
lines: a gun recoiling when a bullet is fired;
a rocket rising as its gases go down.
steps.margin_note: Unmarked, but the question says "examples". Two more lines cost ten seconds.
steps.why: Both are the same physics as the shell: an isolated system that started at rest, splitting into two parts moving opposite ways.
common_mistakes: Writing a long paragraph here when the marks are already earned above.

recall.must_convey: That further examples such as gun recoil or a rocket are named.
reject: shell at rest bursts into two pieces

steps.memory_tip: Gun recoil and rocket motion are the same example with different names: start at rest, split, move apart.

insider_note: Four separate asks, one mark each: momentum, impulse, the law, the example. The example is the one most often left unfinished.
